prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "Palantir Technologies Inc." (ticker PLTR). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Palantir fits nearly every Rule Breaker trait: it is the top dog and first mover in operational and defense AI software, it has a visionary founder-CEO in Alex Karp, revenue grew 93% in Q2 2026, and it is constantly called overvalued at about 178 times trailing earnings. The weaker traits are a polarizing brand and share-price momentum that only roughly matched the S&P 500 over the full past year, though it beat it strongly over six months.
summaries.buffett: Palantir has strong economics now (82% gross margin, no debt, rising free cash flow) and real switching costs, but it was loss-making until 2023, its technology market changes fast, and it relies on government budgets. At roughly 200 times trailing EV/EBIT there is no margin of safety, so it sits well outside Buffett's price discipline and usual circle of competence.
summaries.munger: Munger would admire the hard-to-copy know-how, founder control and capital-light model, but inverting the problem shows several ways to lose: political backlash, AI commoditization by frontier labs and hyperscalers, and a valuation near 178 times earnings that already prices in years of perfect execution. A great business at a price far above value fails his 'wonderful company at a fair price' test.
summaries.lynch: Palantir is a classic Lynch fast grower with a simple story (software that puts AI to work on an organization's data, revenue guided up about 82% in 2026), but it is anything but overlooked and insiders are steady sellers while the share count creeps up. The P/E of about 178 is far above any sustainable long-term growth rate, so the PEG test fails.
summaries.fisher: Palantir scores well on Fisher's growth points: a long sales runway, management committed to new products (Gotham to Foundry to Apollo to AIP), R&D that has produced the AIP growth wave, an unusually effective bootcamp-driven sales engine and high margins. Weaker points are heavy stock-based dilution and a combative, sometimes opaque relationship with critics.
summaries.graham: Palantir fails almost all of Graham's defensive-investor tests: it has been profitable only since 2023, has never paid a dividend, has no ten-year EPS record, and trades at about 178 times earnings and 55 times book value. Only its strong, debt-free balance sheet passes.
summaries.thiel: Palantir is close to Thiel's model monopoly (he co-founded it): proprietary ontology and accredited classified software, a unique early bet that Silicon Valley should serve defense, perfect timing for the AI shift, a founder team and a proven forward-deployed sales channel. The open questions are whether its tech stays far ahead as frontier labs build agent platforms and how durable its position is over 20 years.
summaries.gerstner: Palantir fits Gerstner's focus on AI platform-shift winners with fast, profitable growth: Rule of 40 score of 155% in Q2 2026, a 62% adjusted operating margin and accelerating revenue. His valuation discipline is the problem, with an enterprise value of about $527B against roughly $4.6B of 2026 adjusted free cash flow guidance.
summaries.druckenmiller: Palantir matches Druckenmiller's taste for accelerating earnings and rising estimates around a big theme: guidance was raised from $7.19B to $8.15B for 2026 and EPS more than tripled year on year. The stock has strong momentum since June, but its extreme valuation makes it sensitive to any change in liquidity or sentiment.
summaries.smith: Palantir is a 'good company' by Terry Smith's tests: high gross margin, very high returns on operating capital, no debt and strong cash conversion, with growth reinvested organically. It fails 'don't overpay' by a wide margin, with a free-cash-flow yield under 1%.
summaries.greenblatt: Palantir has a very high return on capital but a very low earnings yield: trailing operating income of about $2.6B against an enterprise value of about $527B gives an EBIT/EV near 0.5%. It ranks poorly on the Magic Formula.
summaries.akre: Two legs of Akre's three-legged stool look strong: an exceptional business (high margins, switching costs) and talented, owner-like founder management with long reinvestment runways. The price is the weak leg, and heavy stock compensation reduces how much of the value accrues to shareholders.
summaries.pabrai: Palantir is not a Dhandho bet: it is not in a temporary setback, it is not cheap, and at about 178 times earnings the downside if growth slows is large. Pabrai's 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' test fails.
summaries.wood: Palantir fits Cathie Wood's framework closely as a leader in AI software that combines AI, cloud data and autonomous defense systems, with an addressable market that could grow many times over as AI agents spread. ARK's own conviction rests on such companies compounding revenue at very high rates for years.
summaries.ackman: Palantir has several Ackman traits (a dominant, capital-light, high-margin business with a large moat and no debt), but its revenue depends heavily on government budgets rather than being simple and predictable, and its valuation offers no discount to intrinsic value. It does not fit his usual buy criteria.
summaries.sleep: Palantir shows parts of Nick Sleep's scale-economics-shared idea (it uses free bootcamps and forward-deployed engineers to make adoption easy), but it keeps very high margins rather than passing scale savings to customers through lower prices. Its 10-20 year position could be stronger if AIP becomes the standard operating layer, but that is not yet clear.
summaries.valentine: Palantir fits Don Valentine's preference for a huge, growing market and a product that solves a painful problem (integrating data and AI into real operations for militaries and companies). Its early history also shows a contrarian founder team that saw a market others ignored.

momentum.evidence: PLTR rose from $146.93 (Apr 1, 2026 open) to about $208.90 on Oct 14, 2026, about +42% in six months versus about +19% for SPY, but over twelve months it gained about 15% ($181.56 to $208.90), roughly in line with SPY's about 17%.

g4.evidence: Co-founders Alex Karp and Peter Thiel lead and back the company, and partners include the US Army, NATO, Microsoft, Anthropic and Anduril.

g6.evidence: At about 178 times trailing earnings (TTM net income $3,016.7M on 2,568.7M diluted shares, price $208.90) it is routinely called one of the most overvalued large-cap stocks.

simple.evidence: The idea (software that ties an organization's data to AI and decisions) is understandable, but how ontology, AIP and classified deployments create value is hard for a generalist to judge, and it has been profitable only since 2023.

b2.evidence: Revenue grew every year from $1,092.7M (2020) to $4,475.4M (2025), but GAAP operating profit only began in 2023, so the record of consistent profitability is short.

integrity.evidence: Management is candid and capital-light with no debt, but a founder-controlled Class F voting structure, $684.0M of stock compensation in 2025 and steady insider selling weaken alignment with outside owners.

b6.evidence: Palantir builds its products in-house rather than through large acquisitions and has openly refused to copy peers, e.g. avoiding conventional sales teams in favor of bootcamps.

roic.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $2,634.7M on a capital base that is mostly the $9,409.1M cash pile implies very high returns on operating capital with no debt, but the returns are high only since 2024.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 operating cash flow was $2,134.5M versus net income of $1,625.0M, and 2026 adjusted free cash flow is guided at $4.5-4.7B.

b10.evidence: Palantir has paid no dividends and retained all earnings, and its market value has grown far faster than the cumulative profit retained since 2023.

safety.evidence: At a market value of about $537B (diluted) against FY2025 net income of $1,625.0M, the price is far above any conservative estimate of value.

fairprice.evidence: About 178 times trailing earnings and over 100 times 2026 adjusted free cash flow guidance is expensive even for 80%+ growth.

mu5.evidence: The business has no debt and sticky customers, but it could be hurt by government budget cuts, AI commoditization by hyperscalers and frontier labs, political backlash and key-person risk around Alex Karp.

reinvest.evidence: US commercial remaining deal value of $6,238M (up 124%) and a growing AIP pipeline give long runways to reinvest in engineers and products at high returns.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear fast grower: revenue up 93% in Q2 2026 and guided to about 82% growth for 2026 from AI platform adoption.

ly3.evidence: Trailing EPS rose from $0.19 (2024) to $0.63 (2025), faster than the P/E of about 178, but no sustainable long-term growth rate matches a P/E that high.

runway.evidence: US commercial revenue is guided to grow at least 134% in 2026, international and sovereign-AI deals are just starting, and it served only 954 customers at end-2025.

ly7.evidence: Insiders including Alex Karp sell regularly under trading plans, and diluted shares rose from 2,450.8M (2024) to 2,565.2M (2025) and 2,568.7M in Q2 2026.

ly8.evidence: Palantir is among the most discussed and heavily traded stocks in the US and a retail-investor favorite.

fi2.evidence: Palantir moved from Gotham (government) to Foundry (commercial), Apollo (deployment) and AIP (2023), which now drives most of its growth.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $353.5M in H1 2026 supports a product set that took revenue from $1,887.6M in H1 2025 to $3,568.0M in H1 2026.

fi4.evidence: Its AIP bootcamps and forward-deployed engineers closed 220 deals worth at least $1M in Q2 2026, with US commercial TCV up 153% to $2,132M.

longterm.evidence: Karp accepted about two decades of losses to build its platforms and kept investing in AIP, with founder-controlled voting designed for long-term decisions.

gr1.evidence: Palantir is a large company by market value (about $537B) but a mid-sized one by revenue ($4,475.4M in 2025).

ni10.evidence: Palantir lost money every year until 2023 (e.g. net loss of $1,166.4M in 2020).

gr4.evidence: Palantir has never paid a dividend.

eps10.evidence: There is no ten-year EPS record: it listed in 2020 and diluted EPS went from -$1.20 (2020) to $0.63 (2025), so ten-year growth cannot be measured.

gr6.evidence: The price of about $208.90 is roughly 178 times trailing EPS of about $1.17.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 178 times P/B of about 55 (market value about $537B over equity of $9,774.2M) is far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its ontology and accredited classified deployments are far ahead of rivals in defense, but in commercial AI Microsoft, Databricks and Snowflake offer close alternatives.

timing.evidence: The AI agent wave and rising defense budgets arrived just as AIP launched, taking revenue growth from 29% in 2024 to 93% in Q2 2026.

th3.evidence: It began by dominating a small market (intelligence analysis software for US agencies) and expanded into defense programs, commercial operations and enterprise AI.

team.evidence: Co-founder Alex Karp has led it since 2005, with co-founders Peter Thiel (chairman) and Stephen Cohen and CTO Shyam Sankar.

th5.evidence: It has a distinctive distribution machine (forward-deployed engineers, AIP bootcamps, government program-of-record channels) that closed 220 $1M+ deals in Q2 2026.

durable.evidence: Classified accreditations and embedded workflows should last, but rapid AI advances by OpenAI, Anthropic and the hyperscalers make its 10-20 year commercial position uncertain.

th7.evidence: In 2003 it bet that Silicon Valley software should serve defense and intelligence when few tech firms would, and it even sued the US Army in 2016 to sell off-the-shelf software.

trend.evidence: It is a leading beneficiary of enterprise AI adoption and software-defined defense, with US commercial revenue up 149% in Q2 2026.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth accelerated to 93% in Q2 2026, net income attributable rose from $326.7M to $1,061.9M, and 2026 revenue guidance was raised from $7.19B to $8.15B.

dr2.evidence: Growing remaining deal value ($6,238M US commercial) suggests better results ahead, but strong growth is already widely expected and priced in.

dr4.evidence: Rising defense budgets help, and its $9.4B cash earns interest, but as a very highly valued growth stock it is sensitive to higher interest rates.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming catalysts include Q3 2026 results (guided to $2.160-2.164B revenue), new defense programs of record and sovereign-AI contracts.

dr7.evidence: Business momentum supports high conviction, but valuation and political risks make a very large concentrated position risky.

gm.evidence: GAAP gross margin was 82.4% in 2025 and 84.7% in Q2 2026.

fcfyield.evidence: 2026 adjusted free cash flow guidance of $4.5-4.7B against an enterprise value of about $527B is a yield under 1%.

gb2.evidence: Trailing operating income of about $2.6B against an enterprise value of about $527B is an EBIT/EV of about 0.5%.

pa2.evidence: There is no setback: revenue grew 93% in Q2 2026 and the share price is near its 52-week high of $212.94.

pa4.evidence: With the stock at about 178 times earnings, a slowdown in growth could lead to a large and lasting loss; it fell from about $207 to $106 between November 2025 and June 2026.

wo1.evidence: Palantir is a leader in AI software, with AIP driving US commercial revenue up 149% in Q2 2026.

wo2.evidence: Software costs per customer fall with scale (gross margin rose from 67.7% in 2020 to 82.4% in 2025), but Palantir keeps the savings as margin rather than cutting prices.

wo3.evidence: It combines AI with cloud software and autonomous defense systems (through partners like Anduril), but it does not span robotics or energy storage itself.

wo4.evidence: Enterprise and government AI spending is growing fast, and its revenue base of $4.5B (2025) is a small fraction of a market worth hundreds of billions.

ac3.evidence: It is insulated from commodity prices and needs no debt, but government budget cycles and interest-rate-driven valuation swings affect it.

ns1.evidence: Palantir keeps scale benefits as margin (adjusted operating margin of 62% in Q2 2026) rather than lowering prices for customers.

ns4.evidence: If AIP becomes the standard AI operating layer its position would be much stronger in 10-20 years, but competition from hyperscalers and AI labs makes that uncertain.

va2.evidence: It solves a large, painful problem: organizations' data is scattered across thousands of systems, and militaries and companies need it combined to act and use AI safely.
